Convert time series objects to mvgam long format

Source: R/series_to_mvgam.R
series_to_mvgam.Rd

Convert a tsibble, a ts, mts or msts object, or a wide data.frame with a date column into the long data.frame that mvgam() expects: one row per series and time, a series factor and a time column counting steps from the first index value.

Usage

series_to_mvgam(
  series,
  freq = NULL,
  response = NULL,
  index = NULL,
  h = NULL,
  train_prop = NULL
)

Arguments

series

The data to convert. One of:

  • A tsibble (tsibble::tsibble()). Its key variables define the series and its index defines the time grid. Gaps in a regular tsibble become rows with a missing response, as tsibble::fill_gaps(.full = TRUE) builds them. Measured variables other than the response are carried over as covariates, with missing values on those rows. An irregular tsibble keeps its own times, for use with CAR() or ZMVN().

  • A ts, mts or msts object (forecast::msts()). Each column of an mts is a series.

  • A wide data.frame holding one date column and one numeric column per series. Column names become the series levels, in column order.

freq

Optional numeric vector of seasonal periods, in time steps. Each period above 1 adds a column giving the position of each row within that period. Defaults to the periods the object carries: frequency() of a ts, the seasonal.periods of an msts, or tsibble::guess_frequency() of the index.

response

Name of the measured variable to use as the response of a tsibble. Optional when the tsibble has one measured variable. Ignored for other inputs, whose response column is y.

index

Name of the date column of a wide data.frame. Optional when exactly one column has class Date, POSIXt, yearmonth, yearquarter or yearweek.

h

Optional number of final time steps to hold out as test data.

train_prop

Optional proportion of time steps to keep as training data, between 0 and 1. Only one of h and train_prop may be given.

Value

A long data.frame. Its columns are series (a factor), time (an integer for regular data), the response and the original index (index for a ts). Any tsibble key and covariate columns follow, then one season column per period above 1. Rows are ordered by time, then series. With h or train_prop, a list holding data_train and data_test instead.

Details

time counts steps from 1 at the first index value. The position within a seasonal period counts steps from the calendar origin of the index. A monthly index with freq = 12 gives the month number whatever month the data start in. A ts gives cycle(). A single period produces a column named season. Several periods produce season_<period> columns, such as season_7 and season_365.25.

Rows for future times with a missing response, built for example with tsibble::new_data() and bound to the observed data, receive time values that continue the grid. Converting observed and future rows together keeps the two aligned.

Seasonal periods take the same numbers across packages. Monthly data carry frequency = 12 in a ts. A fable season(period = "year") on a monthly tsibble resolves to 12 steps. Both take freq = 12. Daily data with seasonal.periods = c(7, 365.25) in an msts take freq = c(7, 365.25).

A season column feeds a fixed seasonal shape, such as s(season, bs = "cc"). The same periods give LLT() a season whose shape drifts over the years, as trend_formula = ~ LLT(season = 12).

See also

The data article covers the long format and its conversion in more depth. LLT() takes the same periods for a season that drifts.

Other model fitting: check_newdata(), jsdgam(), mvgam(), mvgam_data(), mvgam_formula(), mvgam_multiple(), pivot_detection_array(), pivot_species_matrix(), stancode.mvgam_formula(), update.mvgam()

Author

Nicholas J Clark

Examples

# Monthly airline passengers, holding out the final year
air <- series_to_mvgam(AirPassengers, h = 12)
head(air$data_train)
#>     series time   y    index season
#> 1 series_1    1 112 1949.000      1
#> 2 series_1    2 118 1949.083      2
#> 3 series_1    3 132 1949.167      3
#> 4 series_1    4 129 1949.250      4
#> 5 series_1    5 121 1949.333      5
#> 6 series_1    6 135 1949.417      6

# Two series in one mts
deaths <- series_to_mvgam(cbind(male = mdeaths, female = fdeaths))
levels(deaths$series)
#> [1] "male"   "female"

# A wide data.frame with a date column
wide <- data.frame(
  date = seq(as.Date("2024-01-01"), by = "day", length.out = 28),
  site_a = rpois(28, 5),
  site_b = rpois(28, 8)
)
head(series_to_mvgam(wide))
#>   series time  y       date season
#> 1 site_a    1  8 2024-01-01      5
#> 2 site_b    1  8 2024-01-01      5
#> 3 site_a    2 10 2024-01-02      6
#> 4 site_b    2 11 2024-01-02      6
#> 5 site_a    3  4 2024-01-03      7
#> 6 site_b    3 12 2024-01-03      7

# Next: fit the training data, for example with
# mvgam(y ~ s(season, bs = "cc"), trend_formula = ~ AR(),
#       data = air$data_train)
